mcqs.question: Why can't a lock be implemented safely using two separate ordinary instructions — one to check if it's free, one to set it taken?
options: Because ordinary load and store instructions don't exist on multicore processors
Because two cores can both perform the check and see the lock free before either performs the set, both concluding they acquired it — a race that defeats the lock's purpose
Because compilers automatically insert atomic instructions in place of ordinary ones
Because checking a lock's state always requires a full memory barrier
mcqs.explanation: Splitting check-and-grab into two separate instructions creates a window where two cores can both observe the lock as free and both proceed to take it, which is exactly the race a lock is meant to prevent. Ordinary loads/stores exist fine on multicore CPUs, compilers don't silently substitute atomics, and a memory barrier alone doesn't make an operation atomic.

mcqs.question: What does compare-and-swap (CAS) let a thread do that test-and-set does not?
options: CAS can run on more CPU cores simultaneously than test-and-set
CAS lets a thread update a value only if it still matches an expected value, enabling optimistic 'update if nobody else changed it since I last read it' lock-free algorithms
CAS eliminates the need for any atomic hardware instruction
CAS always executes faster than test-and-set on every processor
mcqs.explanation: CAS's compare-then-swap semantics let code detect whether the value changed since it was last read, which is the basis of retry-based lock-free algorithms — test-and-set only supports unconditional set-and-return-old-value. CAS is still itself an atomic hardware instruction, doesn't scale core count, and relative speed depends on the specific processor and workload.

mcqs.question: In the CAS-based spinlock code, why does 'release' just use a plain store instead of another atomic instruction?
options: Because releasing a lock never actually needs to update memory
Because only the current lock holder ever writes the release value, and every other thread is merely reading (spinning), so there's no concurrent-write race to protect against
Because atomic instructions are only needed for reads, never for writes
Because the compiler automatically upgrades any store adjacent to a CAS into an atomic one
mcqs.explanation: Atomicity is needed specifically to prevent concurrent conflicting writes; release only ever has one writer (the holder) with everyone else just reading, so a plain store is safe. Release does update memory, atomic instructions matter for writes just as much as reads, and compilers don't silently upgrade unrelated stores.

mcqs.question: Why is LL/SC naturally immune to the ABA problem in a way plain CAS is not?
options: LL/SC instructions are simply faster than CAS instructions

SC fails if any write touched the watched address since the LL, even one that changed the value and then changed it back, whereas CAS only compares the final value and can't detect an intervening A→B→A change
LL/SC only works on single-core systems, where ABA cannot occur
CAS cannot be used with pointers, only integers
mcqs.explanation: SC's failure condition is tied to any write to the monitored address, not just a value mismatch, so an A→B→A round trip still causes SC to fail — CAS, which only compares the current value against an expected one, cannot distinguish 'unchanged' from 'changed and changed back.' Relative speed isn't the reason, LL/SC is used on multicore systems specifically, and CAS works fine with pointer-sized values.
